Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

Along the spectrum of losses, from the door keys to the love of one’s life, none is more unimaginable, more incomprehensible in its unnatural violation of being and time, than a parent’s loss of a child.

Ernest Hemingway (July 21, 1899–July 2, 1961) was in his twenties and living in France when he befriend Gerald and Sara Murphy. The couple eventually returned to America when one of their sons fell ill, but it was their other son, Baoth, who died after a savage struggle with meningitis.

Upon receiving the news, the thirty-five-year-old writer sent his friends an extraordinary letter, part consolation for and part consecration of a loss for which there is no salve, found in Shaun Usher’s moving compilation Letters of Note: Grief (public library).

You know there is nothing we can ever say or write… Yesterday I tried to write you and I couldn’t.

It is not as bad for Baoth because he had a fine time, always, and he has only done something now that we all must do. He has just gotten it over with…

About him having to die so young — Remember that he had a very fine time and having it a thousand times makes it no better. And he is spared from learning what sort of a place the world is.

It is your loss: more than it is his, so it is something that you can, legitimately, be brave about. But I can’t be brave about it and in all my heart I am sick for you both.

Absolutely truly and coldly in the head, though, I know that anyone who dies young after a happy childhood, and no one ever made a happier childhood than you made for your children, has won a great victory. We all have to look forward to death by defeat, our bodies gone, our world destroyed; but it is the same dying we must do, while he has gotten it all over with, his world all intact and the death only by accident.

In a breathtaking sentiment evocative of Anaïs Nin’s admonition against the stupor of near-living, and of poet Meghan O’Rourke’s grief-honed conviction that “the people we most love do become a physical part of us, ingrained in our synapses, in the pathways where memories are created,” Hemingway adds:

Very few people ever really are alive and those that are never die; no matter if they are gone. No one you love is ever dead.

With this, echoing Auden’s insistence that “we must love one another or die,” he comes the closest he ever came to formulating the meaning of life. Like David Foster Wallace, who addressed the meaning of life with such exquisite lucidity shortly before he was slain by depression, Hemingway too would lose hold of that meaning in the throes of the agony that would take his life a quarter century later. Now, from the fortunate platform of the prime of life, he writes:

We must live it, now, a day at a time and be very careful not to hurt each other. It seems as though we were all on a boat together, a good boat still, that we have made but that we know will never reach port. There will be all kinds of weather, good and bad, and especially because we know now that there will be no landfall we must keep the boat up very well and be very good to each other. We are fortunate we have good people on the boat.

Complement with the young Dostoyevsky’s exultation about the meaning of life shortly after his death sentence was repealed, Emily Dickinson on love and loss, Thoreau on living through loss, and Nick Cave — who lived, twice, the unimaginable tragedy of the Murphys — on grief as a portal to aliveness, then revisit the fascinating neuroscience of your brain on grief and your heart on healing.

#9386. The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

A major new study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.

Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces showed lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.

James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.

To gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.

"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.

How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity

McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.

"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland says.

The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.

During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.

They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.

The results showed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.

"The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," says first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.

The researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.

"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.

Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought

Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers new insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.

Recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.

Much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.

By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.

"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland says.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support

The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.

Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.

An ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.

"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.

Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.

However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.

"Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland says. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people."

New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis

Another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Currently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.

Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.

The newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.

Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.

"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland says.

#9385. Why Sending Reels Is More Meaningful Than You Think

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Humans are constantly reinventing ways to maintain intimacy with the people we care about most. Today, one of our most ubiquitous connection rituals is reel sharing—that is, sending short social media videos to each other. At a time when much of the conversation about technology centers on how it is eroding human connection, reel sharing and the unspoken social norms that surround it suggest another possibility: a tool to maintain social bonds.

This has been my experience. I met my best friend of more than 25 years, Kyra, when I was a Peace Corps volunteer. Our friendship formed before social media and with geographic distance between us (she served in Togo and I was in Cameroon). During Peace Corps service, we mainly stayed in touch through sporadic emails. After Peace Corps, we both started careers in international development, got married, and had a few kids. Our geographic separation didn’t change, but our time to email and chat on the phone did, significantly limiting our communication. I missed her.

A couple of years ago, we started sending each other reels through Facebook (her preference) and Instagram (my preference). It became our version of “I’m thinking of you” or “Here’s something to brighten your day”—an asynchronous way of staying connected, sharing our interests, and quietly checking our emotional attunement with one another. Sending reels has helped to strengthen our friendship at a cadence that works for our busy lives.

But there’s a tension with this practice, which is the guilt I sometimes feel about spending so much time on social media. Though an estimated 37–71% of Americans use social media sites, many have turned against them altogether, inviting us to throw out both the baby and the bathwater. Indeed, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram (Meta) recently settled a lawsuit (for billions of dollars) that alleged that their sites were intentionally designed to addict children and teens.

There might be good reasons to restrain social media use, but people will continue to use it—and so the question becomes: How can they use it wisely? Perhaps repositioning social media reel sending as a ritual of connection can help to recalibrate how and why we engage with the platform.

Social science sees interpersonal rituals as repetitive, symbolic actions that foster belonging and communicate shared meaning. Such rituals are routinized actions or behaviors that have unspoken norms understood by the participants. Performing the ritual with others symbolizes their importance in our lives and creates an opportunity for shared meaning, which collectively reinforces the bond.

Sending reels has become a modernized form of relationship maintenance, done to keep a relationship alive, relevant, and emotionally present. Relationship maintenance is a behavior we engage in to show our commitment to a relationship. There are both routine and strategic forms of relationship maintenance. We employ these tactics across all types of relationships: romantic, platonic, familial, and professional.

Routine maintenance consist of frequent, intuitive acts done to stay connected to the person through regular communication and information sharing—as opposed to grander gestures like buying flowers and other gifts, showing up at difficult moments, or bringing someone to the airport.

The reason we feel irritated when our reel sending doesn’t receive a reaction is because relationships are rooted in social exchange. Essentially, relationships are based on a subconscious cost-benefit analysis, where reciprocity is expected, although not explicitly stated. Behaviors that are rewarded will continue—but the absence of reward can harm the relationship.

Perhaps you’re a mom who recently started sending reels to your adult daughter to reinforce regular communication. You’ll likely continue to do so until you realize, “Wait, she hasn’t responded.” While the action of sending reels is something we may do without much thought, we expect acknowledgment of the gesture: a like, emoji, comment, or reciprocal sending. When we don’t receive that, we feel disappointed. But when we do get the anticipated response, we feel closer to the person.

Kyra and I use a combination of emojis and reciprocal sending to signify reception. We’re so committed to reciprocal sending, that the other day she sent me this reel to remind me what to do if a couple of days went by without her sending me anything!

Think about the last person you sent a reel to. Who was it? I’m willing to bet they were a close friend, relative, or romantic partner. That’s because reels are typically shared with someone you care about, someone you want to be in community with, and the goal is to reinforce closeness.

While research focused on sending reels as a form of digital communication is scarce, we can extrapolate the link between relationship closeness and reel-sending behavior from studies focused on digital memes (static photos) and GIFs (looping animations).

Researchers asked 395 study participants, ranging in age from 18 to 75, to recall situations where they sent a text message to a strong tie (close relationship) and a weak tie (acquaintance) and report their use of graphic icons such as memes, GIFs, and emojis. Participants reported more sharing with strong ties than weak ties.

Those who used graphic icons more frequently reported greater feelings of self-disclosure (“I can talk to X about anything”), relationship maintenance (We “try to make each other laugh”), and intimacy (“How often do you tell your friend everything that you are going through?”).

Admittedly, sending a reel to someone requires a bit of vulnerability.

You are taking a risk by sending something that resonates with you, but you aren’t 100% sure will resonate and be reciprocated by the other person. The likelihood of success depends on how accurately you guessed the person’s likes or dislikes.

The vulnerability factor is another reason we are more likely to send reels to close others; vulnerability typically follows closeness, not the other way around. When we are vulnerable with people we are close to, the risk is diminished because we know them better. If it fails, the potential harm is cushioned by our established relationship.

Aside from the vulnerability factor, there’s a reason when you’re scrolling social media that you don’t see a reel and immediately think to send it to Bob in accounting or your dentist. While they may be cool people, they simply aren’t top of mind for you.

Close relationships carry emotional weight, and our brain is much more likely to remember emotionally salient information. For example, Kyra has three very active sons who all play competitive sports. Her weekends are consumed with sporting events, so every time I see a post about sports moms, I think of her and send it. It’s my way of recognizing her efforts and sacrifice.

Reels are digital objects that can trigger us to think of others. Because we have much more information about close relationships and cognitively our experiences with them are more accessible, when we want to share a reel, we pick from this list of people.

Shared experiences are an important component of fostering connections, serving as the foundation for establishing shared meaning. When you’re in the same physical space, this might look like watching movies together, attending events, or sharing meals.

Reels offer an asynchronous substitute for shared experiences. By viewing a reel, and maybe even sharing a brief commentary on it, and then sending it to a connection who then reacts, you are creating a digital shared experience—viewing and reacting to the same content.

Shared experiences help us to understand the preferences and thoughts of others, while sharing our own. Through this exchange, we can align our minds and create shared meaning. It’s a form of emotional attunement, a core component of close social connection.

Sending reels tests out that alignment. Essentially, when we send reels, we are saying, “I found this to be funny, did you?” or “This really resonated with me, how about you?”  or “I thought this information would be useful to you, is it?” The validation of alignment is in the receiver’s reaction.

When distance or busyness prevent or limit in-person interaction, sending reels allows us to share funny, thought-provoking, or motivational content with people we care about, maintaining a sense of closeness, having laughed, gasped, or become angry at the same reel. We reinforce connection through mutual understanding and shared meaning.

If you send reels and you’ve categorized it as a “guilty pleasure,” I’d encourage you to reconsider the guilt part. Guilt suggests you are doing something bad when the intention and the value behind sending the reel is likely anything but.

The all-or-nothing culture of social media today doesn’t give space for a more nuanced look at our productive use of these platforms and overlooks that some of our online engagement reflects values-based behaviors.

The question is not simply how much time we spend on social media, but what we are doing there. Compulsive scrolling and intentionally connecting with someone we care about may occur on the same platform, but they are not the same.

So, keep sending the reels, not as the only sign that you care, but as one of many in your interpersonal toolbox. I know Kyra and I don’t plan on stopping anytime soon!

#9384. The Souls of Animals

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. “They do not sweat and whine about their condition,” Walt Whitman wrote of the other animals, “they do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins, they do not make me sick discussing their duty to God, not one is dissatisfied, not one is demented with the mania of owning things.”

Here was “the poet of the body and the poet of the soul” holding up a mirror to us creatures inhabiting an animal body complicated by a soul — that organ of want and worry which we ourselves invented to explain why we make art, why we fall in love, why we yearn to converse with reality in prayers and postulates.

It is daring enough to ask what a soul actually is. Carl Jung knew that it defies the substance we are made of: “The soul is partly in eternity and partly in time.” Virginia Woolf knew that it defies our best technology of thought: “One can’t write directly about the soul. Looked at, it vanishes.” It is doubly daring to question the age-old dogma that the soul is the province of the human animal alone. Even as we have incrementally and reluctantly admitted other creatures into the temple of consciousness, we have denied them souls — denied them, because our tools of communication and computation have failed to probe it, an inner life capable of imagination and play, of love and grief, of dreams and wonder. And yet our very language defies our denial: the word animal comes from the Latin for soul.

In 1991, long before we came to consider the soul of an octopus, long before fMRI and EEG studies revealed not only that birds dream but what they dream about, Gary Kowalski took up this daring question in The Souls of Animals (public library) — an inquiry into the “spiritual lives” (and into what that means) of whooping cranes, elephants, jackdaws, gorillas, songbirds, horses, dogs, and cats. At its center is the idea that spirituality — which he defines as “the development of a moral sense, the appreciation of beauty, the capacity for creativity, and the awareness of one’s self within a larger universe as well as a sense of mystery and wonder about it all” — is a natural byproduct of “the biological order and in the ecology shared by all life.” (There are in this view echoes of Kepler, who believed that the Earth itself is an ensouled body, and of myriad native cosmogonies that regard other animals as sources of more-than-human wisdom and emissaries of the numinous.)

Kowalski — a parish minister by vocation, who spends his days praying with the dying, blessing bonds of love, and helping people navigate moral quandaries — celebrates the soul as “the magic of life,” as that which “gives life its sublimity and grandeur,” and reflects:

For ancient peoples, the soul was located in the breath or the blood. For me, soul resides at the point where our lives intersect with the timeless, in our love of goodness, our passion for beauty, our quest for meaning and truth. In asking whether animals have souls, we are inquiring whether they share in the qualities that make life more than a mere struggle for survival, endowing existence with dignity and élan.

Many people think of soul as the element of personality that survives bodily death, but for me it refers to something much more down-to-earth. Soul is the marrow of our existence as sentient, sensitive beings. It’s soul that’s revealed in great works of art, and soul that’s lifted up in awe when we stand in silence under a night sky burning with billions of stars. When we speak of a soulful piece of music, we mean one that comes out of infinite depths of feeling. When we speak of the soul of a nation, we mean its capacity for valor and visionary change… Soul is present wherever our lives intersect the dimension of the holy: in moments of intimacy, in flights of fancy, and in rituals that hallow the evanescent events of our lives with enduring significance. Soul is what makes each of our lives a microcosm — not merely a meaningless fragment of the universe, but at some level a reflection of the whole.

Half a century after Henry Beston insisted that “we need another and a wiser and perhaps a more mystical concept of animals,” for they are “gifted with extensions of the senses we have lost or never attained, living by voices we shall never hear,” Kowalski writes:

Without anthropomorphizing our nonhuman relations we can acknowledge that animals share many human characteristics. They have individual likes and dislikes, moods and mannerisms, and possess their own integrity, which suffers when not respected. They play and are curious about their world. They develop friendships and sometimes risk their own lives to help others. They have “animal faith,” a spontaneity and directness that can be most refreshing… all the traits indicative of soul. For soul is not something we can see or measure. We can observe only its outward manifestations: in tears and laughter, in courage and heroism, in generosity and forgiveness. Soul is what’s behind-the-scenes in the tough and tender moments when we are most intensely and grippingly alive.

By investigating the inner lives of other creatures, Kowalski argues, we are invariably deepening our own:

As [modern] shamans, we are allowed to examine enigmas like “What makes us human?” and “What makes life sacred?” We can ask not only about the mating behavior and survival strategies of other animals but whether they have souls and spirits like our own. The danger here is that we are often in over our heads. But at least we are swimming in deep water and out of the shallows. In searching for answers to such queries, I have found, we not only enrich our understanding of other creatures, we also gain insight into ourselves.

There is an inwardness in other living beings that awakens what is innermost in ourselves. I have often marveled, for instance, watching a flock of shore birds. On an invisible cue, they simultaneously rise off the beach and into the air, then turn and bank seawards in tight formation. They are so finely coordinated and attuned in their aeronautics it is as though they share a common thought, or even a group mind, guiding their ascent. At such moments, I feel there are depths of “inner space” in nature that can never be sounded. And it is out of those same depths, in me, that awe arises as I contemplate the synchronicity of their flight. To contain such depths is to participate in the realm of spirit.

We have invented no greater expression of our inwardness than music — the language of the soul, with its eternal translation between mathematics and mystery. We know that other animals partake of that language — each spring birds sing the world back to life, each summer cicadas serenade the sun with their living mandolin, and when we set out to tell the cosmos who we are, a whale song joined Bulgarian folk music and Bach on The Golden Record.

Birds, Kowalski observes, sing for reasons beyond the pragmatic — their song is “far from a mechanical performance” and “much more complex than a simple cry of self-assertion.” It is music, which is distinguished from noise by an organizing principle of creative intent, and creativity may be the purest evidence of soul. Kowalski writes:

Surprisingly, many birds are relatively insensitive to pitch. But the best singers employ all the elements of tone, interval, rhythm, theme, and variation in complex and highly pleasing combinations. And what is music if not the deliberate arrangement of sound in aesthetic patterns?

Greatly influenced by philosopher Martin Buber’s I-Thou model of relating, Kowalski admonishes against relying on our own frames of reference in assaying what other creatures are expressing and how it is being expressed:

The tempo of life is faster-paced for birds than for people. This is one of the reasons the individual notes in bird song are so short, sometimes distinguishable only with a spectrograph, and why the compositions of birds last a few seconds at most, compared to an hour or more for a human symphony. It is also why birds sing in the upper registers (just as the pitch on a phonograph record rises when played at high speed). To the birds, with a metabolism continually in allegro, human beings must appear to be lazy and dim-brained creatures indeed. Just as our music reflects the rhythm and intensity of our inner life, the music of birds expresses the flash and flutter of their nervous and high-strung existence.

Examining another subset of the creative impulse — visual art — Kowalski cites Desmond Morris’s famous 1950s studies, which found that non-human primates given pens and paints not only became adept at using them with “a distinct feel for symmetry and balance,” but developed individual styles of drawing. He considers what that indicates:

Art arises from a spiritual longing that all people share: to make our mark on the world and to spend our life energy in a work that rises above the mundane, adding grace to existence. We respond to the light of the world around us by giving expression to our own inner light, and when the two are on the same wavelength, the world seems more brilliant and finely focused.

Insisting that such spiritual longings do not belong to human beings alone, he cites an astonishing case study:

In 1982 Jerome Witkin, a professor of art at Syracuse University and a respected authority on abstract expressionism, was invited to view a collection of drawings by a “mystery artist.” The professor was busy at the time, preparing for a traveling exhibition. Nevertheless, he was sufficiently intrigued to accept the invitation.

“These drawings are very lyrical, very, very beautiful,” the professor said when he saw the portfolio. “They are so positive and affirmative and tense, the energy is so compact and controlled, it’s just incredible.”

“This piece is so graceful, so delicate,” he said of one drawing. “I can’t get most of my students to fill a page like this.”

Only after he had finished his professional evaluation did Witkin learn the identity of the artist: a fourteen-year-old, 8,400-pound Asian elephant named Siri who lived in Syracuse’s Burnet Park Zoo. Siri’s keeper, David Gucwa, had seen her tracing lines with sticks and stones in the dust of her cage. Against the wishes of the zoo’s superintendent, who scoffed at the notion of an artistic elephant, Gucwa had given her pads of paper and charcoal, permitting her to express herself more freely.

When Witkin showed Siri’s drawings to a colleague without context — an expert on children’s drawings charing the university’s art education department — she firmly concluded that they were not done by a child. Witkin himself readily likened them to the work of Willem de Kooning, wishing the painter himself could see Siri’s art.

It was this report of Siri that inspired May Sarton — one of my favorite poets and favorite thinkers — to reimagine these reckonings in a poem. (The footnote of credit in Sarton’s collection is how I discovered Kowalski’s book.)

The drawings were abstract, Delicate, Like Japanese calligraphy. When the painter de Kooning Was shown them, he said, “Interesting. Not done by a child, I think, Or if so, an extraordinary child.” “The artist is an elephant, Sir, Named Siri.”

It had once come about That the keeper noticed Her sensitive trunk Drawing designs in the dust. After an argument With the head of the zoo Who laughed at him, The keeper himself Brought large sheets of paper And boxes of charcoal And laid them at Siri’s feet. For an hour at a time In happy concentration The elephant created designs. Like Japanese calligraphy. What artist’s hand As skillful As that sensuous, sensitive trunk?

Two decades after Iris Murdoch found psychological symmetry between art and morality, locating in both “an occasion for unselfing,” Kowlaski turns to the acts of selflessness and compassion that evince a moral faculty — that fundament of a soul. Pelicans and crows, he notes, have been known to care for blind comrades. Darwin himself reported of a band of monkeys coming to the aid of member seized by an eagle, at the risk of their own lives. But nothing renders such morally tinted actions more vivid and more moving than one nineteenth-century naturalist’s account of a misfire.

Working in an era when “collecting specimens” meant killing creatures, he aimed at a tern but only wounded the bird, which fell helplessly into the sea. Immediately, other terns began circling above “manifesting much apparent solicitude,” until two of them dove down toward their wounded comrade. They lifted him up, one at each wing, carried him several yards, and gently put him down before another two picked him up, and so the group took turns carrying him the entire distance to the shore. The naturalist was so moved by this display of compassion and solidarity that, although he was within shot of the rock on which the wounded tern had been rested, he couldn’t bring himself to finish what he had set out to do.

To witness such a scene is to be stilled with wonder and with humility — which, as Rachel Carson so poignantly wrote, “are wholesome emotions, and they do not exist side by side with a lust for destruction.” A generation after her, and well ahead of our still dawning awakening to the ecological and ethical dignity of other species, Kowalaski reflects:

If we are to keep our family homestead — third stone from the sun — safe for coming generations, we must awaken to a new respect for the family of life.

We are kin to, and must be kind to, all creation. Overcoming speciesism — the illusion of human superiority — will be the next step in our moral and spiritual evolution.

To behold such a display of moral feeling with our own eyes is stirring enough, but to be witnessed back by another creature’s eyes is nothing short of a spiritual experience. In a passage that calls to mind Alan Lightman’s transcendent account of looking into the eyes of an osprey, Kowalski writes:

It is difficult to probe the inward awareness of another being. The realm of what one mystic called “the interior castle” is wholly private and wrapped in solitude. But when we look into another’s eyes — even into the eyes of an animal — we may find a small window into that inner sanctum, a window through which our souls can hail and greet one another.

The act of making eye contact with another being presupposes a conscious self behind either pair of peepers: I see you seeing me, and I am aware that you are aware that we are looking at each other.

Perhaps in the end it is not we who have the power to acknowledge or deny the souls of other creatures but other creatures who confer soul-ness upon us. Kowalski writes:

If by soul we mean our sense of self, our identity as particular persons, then our souls are interwoven with those of other living beings… We know ourselves as human, in part, through our relationships with the nonhuman world.

We are rather unsure of ourselves. What distinguishes our species may be this inward anxiety. While other animals may be endowed with special gifts—acute hearing, keen eyesight, incredible speed — human beings are nothing special. This is both a biological and a moral judgment. Lack of specialization makes us highly adaptable, but it also means we have no fixed form or definite identity. Without many inborn instincts to guide us, we as human beings need models for how to live. We need a sense of our own possibilities and limits, and we find them not only in the artificial rules and restraints imposed by human society but in the lessons for living suggested by biology and the earth itself. We are the younger siblings in life’s family — the perpetual neonates of the animal world. In a fundamental way we need other creatures to tell us who we are.

Out of this arises an urgency more than ethical, more than ecological, but existential — nothing less than examining what we are and why we are here at all:

What profit do we have if we gain the whole world and lose or forfeit our own souls? The human race may survive without the chimpanzees, orangutans, and other wild creatures who share the planet. But we will have attenuated the conditions that are necessary for our own “ensoulment”… And when we look into the mirror there will be less and less to love.

There is a glimmering of eternity about our lives. In the vastness of time and space, our lives are indeed small and ephemeral, yet not utterly insignificant. Our lives do matter. Because we care for one another and have feelings, because we can dream and imagine, because we are the kinds of creatures who make music and create art, we are not merely disconnected fragments of the universe but at some level reflect the beauty and splendor of the whole. And because all life shares in One Spirit, we can recognize this indwelling beauty in other creatures.

Couple The Souls of Animals with John James Audubon — who was both a visionary ahead of his time and, like the tern-shooting naturalist, a product of its blind spots — on other minds and the secret knowledge of animals, then revisit Loren Eiseley on the wonder of being alive lensed through a bouquet of warblers and a reflection on signs vs. omens and our search for meaning lensed through a great blue heron.

#9383. Four Levels Of Customer Understanding

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Many companies think they know fairly well what their users want and need, and how they make their decisions. Yet most of the time these are merely big assumptions and big hunches — with little real evidence to support them. In practice, obvious reasons might be true, but they rarely paint the full picture.

To understand our customers, we must triangulate across four levels of customer understanding by Hannah Shamji. It’s a useful way to think about the underlying reasons for user behavior, hidden motivations, and the complex layers of messy and noisy reality that are often overlooked. Let’s see how it works.

To learn about customers, it might seem reasonable to ask people what they think and draw conclusions from it. But it’s rarely an effective way to get actionable answers. In fact, as it turns out, what people think, feel, say, and do are often very different things.

As Erika Hall wrote, asking a question directly is the worst way to get a true and useful answer to that question. We don’t always understand or are aware of our true motivations. We often apply our own context and interpretations to questions.

We also exaggerate (a lot!). We focus on edge cases and unrealistic scenarios, and we favor short-term goals over long-term goals. So if users say that they absolutely need to compare products in a table, it doesn’t mean that they couldn’t get to their underlying goal without it.

Just to indicate how tricky listening to words alone is: even little nuances in words chosen matter. In practice, users are rarely precise in expressing their thoughts, and a good example is the distinction between possible, plausible, and probable, as discovered by Thomas D’hooge.

A study on Dutch verbal probability terms shows how unreliable the choice of words is. While extreme words have some agreement, terms like “possible,” “maybe,” “uncertain,” or “likely” lead to a wide spread of interpretations. So we shouldn’t rely on what people say, but rather try to go deeper.

To get a more realistic and less biased view of customers’ needs, we need to understand a broader picture across 4 levels:

Personally, I wouldn’t recommend NPS (alternative). It’s worth noting that different levels might reveal conflicting or contradictory data. To get a better understanding, we need to triangulate and reconcile data with mixed-method research.

Emotions are always difficult to capture, but they are easier to spot once you observe people doing what they need to do without external influence or interruptions. The ability to positively impact users grows by moving from sympathy to empathy or even compassion, as articulated by Sarah Gibbons.

In the past, I was using “speak-aloud” protocol and asked users to walk me through their thought process as they were completing tasks. But it actually turns out to be quite disruptive. Because people are focused on speaking at the same time while solving a task, many emotions remain hidden or obscured by their language.

So, when conducting usability testing, I don’t ask users to speak through their experience. Instead, I observe where they tap or hover with the mouse, where their mouse circles without an action, where they scroll, and how long. Eventually, when a user confirms that they are done or that they are stuck, I ask questions.

The Emotion Wheel (website) by Geoffrey Roberts is a helpful little tool for better describing a range of emotions during user interviews or design sessions. It certainly needs refinement for product design needs, but it helps us get more precise about the sentiment customers or colleagues might be experiencing, moving beyond just “good” or “bad”.

One helpful trick is to use mirroring — repeating what a user has said, or ask the same question twice, just paraphrasing it. Or navigating the emotions wheel (see above) to better capture and understand the emotion.

These strategies help uncover some of the issues that perhaps didn’t come up in the first answer. That’s also when a user tends to add more useful context and details as they explain their confusion.

I think that Alin brings up a very strong argument, and personally, I find it difficult to disagree with. However, I do see user’s emotional response as a signal of how well the product is working for them. How engaged or detached they are in their journey, how they react to aesthetics, how confused or confident they are.

Ultimately, these are signals. To make a difference, we must go beyond emotions and explore what people actually do. Usually, this means relentlessly observing, diagnosing, and focusing on underlying user needs.

Instead of asking, we need to observe. Usually, I focus on small things that make or break an experience. I see where users lose time, repeat actions, hover without clicking, or click and then go back. Pay attention to subtle cues like scratching their neck, raising eyebrows, or expressions of worry, joy, or confusion.

Many companies talk about “validation” through user testing, but often that means simply confirming existing assumptions. But we should instead diagnose existing behavior without preconceived notions or affiliations. We don’t validate — we actually research instead.

That research means not just understanding customers’ real motivations, but also risks, doubts, concerns, worries, and perhaps even harms.

The only way to get there is by building a sincere, honest, and trustworthy relationship — one that feels right and resonates deeply. When customers truly care and want to help, getting to a real understanding becomes much, much easier.

We don’t need expensive tools to uncover user needs. David Travis provides a fantastic overview of helpful strategies to do just that. Here are some initiatives to spread the word about real user’s struggles or gain a deeper understanding of user needs:

The core idea here is that you don’t need extensive and expensive tools to uncover user needs. You need to create spaces where customers’ struggles can be exposed and make these struggles visible across the entire company.

It can be short video clips of user sessions or a monthly newsletter with what we learned this month. Making these pain points visible can rally everyone from marketing to engineering to keep users’ struggles at the back of their minds.

To make an impact, we must go way beyond user feedback. It’s never enough to listen to surveys — we must observe customers’ actual behaviors and build relationships to truly understand their goals and their motivations.

And most importantly, we need to understand what questions we actually want to have answered. Not what “validation” we need to move on with the project, but what we don’t know and what we need to research.

Without it, everything else is merely hunches and assumptions — and often wrong and expensive ones.

#9382. Charles Dickens’s writing chalet and Hastings Castle added to list of English heritage sites at risk

Left: Charles Dickens' Writing Chalet, Rochester, Kent. Right: Hastings Castle

Dickens’ chalet: Photo: Nick Johnson - The Imageworks. Hastings Castle: © Historic England Archive

The cabin where Charles Dickens spent the last day of his life, the home in Stratford-upon-Avon of William Shakespeare’s daughter Susanna and the castle built by William the Conqueror high on the cliffs above the town of Hastings are among 197 buildings and sites added to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register today (5 November).

The list identifies sites such as buildings, parks, battlefields and shipwrecks that are threatened by decay, neglect or inappropriate development. There are now 4,991 entries on the register, all of which are labelled as of national importance. This encompasses 197 sites that were added this year.

The miniature Swiss chalet which became the writing retreat of Charles Dickens was a Christmas gift to the author in 1864, arrived flat packed in 94 pieces, and was put together by a theatre carpenter after Dickens and his house guests failed. Dickens placed it at the furthest end of the garden, reached by a tunnel he built under the road at his last home, Gad’s Hill, near Rochester in Kent. He spent much of 9 June 1870 working in the chalet on The Mystery of Edwin Drood, before returning to the house where he died that night, aged just 58.The house, now a school, and tunnel survive, but the chalet was moved in the 1960s to the garden of Eastgate House in Rochester, where it is now too fragile for public access.

Hall’s Croft, an imposing timber-framed building dating from 1613, was the home of Susanna Shakespeare and her husband John Hall. After many uses, and residents including the playwright George Bernard Shaw and the bestselling Victorian romantic novelist Marie Corelli, it was acquired by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and opened to the public in 1951. It had already been closed for several years for extensive conservation work when, in October 2025, a car reversed into the facade and caused further serious damage. The playwright Ken Ludwig has donated £1m to the work but major fundraising will still be needed.

Hall’s Croft, Old Town, Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire

Hastings Castle was one of the first three such sites built by William the Conqueror after his victory in the famous battle—and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. The site, with a sweeping view across a stretch of the coast, has a long history, with remains of an Iron Age fort having been discovered there. The castle’s commanding site has made it very vulnerable to storms and coastal erosion and there have already been urgent works to stabilise its ruins. Future plans for the site include the creation of a new visitor centre and cafe.

Along with the sites that have been added this year there is good news: 85 sites for which solutions have been found, and which have now been removed from the register. They include the storm-lashed Newlyn Harbour in Cornwall and a little hut in the Gloucestershire garden of Edward Jenner, in which, in 1796, he performed the first-ever vaccinations.

A pair of elegant Georgian houses in east London, built around 1715 and Grade II* listed, had an unusual saviour: Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, which has converted them—with help from the Lottery Heritage Fund—into artists studios, gallery spaces, and a cafe. The space is run by Sarabande Foundation, which was founded by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen.

The Georgian terraced house saved from dereliction by Tottenham Hotspur FC. The house is now home to artists’ studios, galleries and café run by Sarabande Foundation, which was established by Lee Alexander McQueen

Rescue grants available include the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund and the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, both funded by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and administered by Historic England, and the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service.

The UK’s heritage minister Baroness Twycross said in a statement that the register has a crucial role in identifying historic places in need of support. “Every part of the UK is bursting with history, so it is vital we protect the heritage sites at the heart of communities which help tell the stories of our nation.”

Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire, the joint chief executives of Historic England, said the most effective way of protecting the sites was to bring them back into use.“The sites saved and removed from the Register this year show what can be achieved when partners and communities work together to deliver positive lasting change.”

Taylor’s in Loughborough faces uphill struggle in fundraising drive to restore decaying buildings and create new museum

#9381. Umberto Eco’s Antilibrary: Why Unread Books Are More Valuable to Our Lives than Read Ones

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

“It is our knowledge — the things we are sure of — that makes the world go wrong and keeps us from seeing and learning,” Lincoln Steffens wrote in his beautiful 1925 essay. Piercingly true as this may be, we’ve known at least since Plato’s famous Allegory of the Cave that “most people are not just comfortable in their ignorance, but hostile to anyone who points it out.”. Although science is driven by “thoroughly conscious ignorance” and the spiritual path paved with admonitions against the illusion of thorough understanding, we cling to our knowledge — our incomplete, imperfect, infinitesimal-in-absolute-terms knowledge — like we cling to life itself.

And yet the contour of what we know is a mere silhouette cast by the infinite light of the unknown against the screen of the knowable. The great E.F. Schumacher captured this strange dynamic in the concept of adaequatio — the notion that “the understanding of the knower must be adequate to the thing to be known.” But how do we face our inadequacy with grace and negotiate wisely this eternal tension between the known, the unknown, the knowable, and the unknowable?

That’s what Lebanese-American scholar, statistician, and essayist Nassim Nicholas Taleb explores in a section of his modern classic The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable (public library) — an illuminating inquiry into the unknowable and unpredictable outlier-events that precipitate profound change, and our tendency to manufacture facile post-factum explanations for them based on our limited knowledge.

Taleb uses legendary Italian writer Umberto Eco’s uncommon relationship with books and reading as a parable of the most fruitful relationship with knowledge:

The writer Umberto Eco belongs to that small class of scholars who are encyclopedic, insightful, and nondull. He is the owner of a large personal library (containing thirty thousand books), and separates visitors into two categories: those who react with “Wow! Signore professore dottore Eco, what a library you have! How many of these books have you read?” and the others — a very small minority — who get the point that a private library is not an ego-boosting appendage but a research tool. Read books are far less valuable than unread ones. The library should contain as much of what you do not know as your financial means, mortgage rates, and the currently tight real-estate market allows you to put there. You will accumulate more knowledge and more books as you grow older, and the growing number of unread books on the shelves will look at you menacingly. Indeed, the more you know, the larger the rows of unread books. Let us call this collection of unread books an antilibrary.

Eco himself has since touched on humanity’s curious relationship with the known and the unknown in his encyclopedia of imaginary lands, the very existence of which is another symptom of our compulsive tendency to fill in the gaps of our understanding with concrete objects of “knowledge,” even if we have to invent them by the force of our imagination. Taleb adds:

We tend to treat our knowledge as personal property to be protected and defended. It is an ornament that allows us to rise in the pecking order. So this tendency to offend Eco’s library sensibility by focusing on the known is a human bias that extends to our mental operations. People don’t walk around with anti-résumés telling you what they have not studied or experienced (it’s the job of their competitors to do that), but it would be nice if they did. Just as we need to stand library logic on its head, we will work on standing knowledge itself on its head.

Noting that his Black Swan theory centers on “our misunderstanding of the likelihood of surprises” because we underestimate the value of what we don’t know and take what we do know “a little too seriously,” Taleb envisions the perfect dancer in the tango with knowledge:

Let us call this an antischolar — someone who focuses on the unread books, and makes an attempt not to treat his knowledge as a treasure, or even a possession, or even a self-esteem enhancement device — a skeptical empiricist.

Complement The Black Swan, which is fascinating it its totality, with astrophysicist Marcelo Gleiser on how to live with mystery in a culture obsessed with certitude, philosopher Hannah Arendt on how unanswerable questions give shape to the human experience, and novelist Marilynne Robinson on the beauty of the unknown.

Every month, I spend hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars keeping The Marginalian going. For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. #9380. How Positive Psychology Can Influence Public Policy

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Imagine a medical doctor who never goes to the clinic and never publicizes availability for care. Instead, the doctor provides care when close friends need help or when an emergency occurs in their presence. While these acts are good in and of themselves, one could not help but wonder whether the doctor’s approach maximizes their potential positive impact.

Positive psychologists often act like that. Like the doctor, we have specialized knowledge. We run studies and test theories. We accomplish things in our smaller circles. But without diminishing the value of these acts, one cannot help—as with our imaginary doctor—but wonder whether we could sometimes do more.

While influencing public policy is not the only means to “do more,” it is (we believe) an undervalued avenue. Public policymakers are, to some degree, in need of the very thing we can (but often do not) provide.

Consider that public policy creators confront conflicting requests. Some voices ask for dismantling of camps for the unhoused, while others favor leniency. Some want programming to address the mental health of all schoolkids, while others worry these programs distract from education or may even be harmful. Others want more dollars for police enforcement while still others want less. Policy creators thus often want guidance. Absent guidance, they might follow their intuition or the most confident-sounding “researcher.” Psychologists can help.

How best to help? In this piece, we briefly explore three ways that positive psychology can impact public policy.

Public officials often focus on brass-tacks issues such as better housing, education, transit, recreation opportunities, or public safety.

However, their impact on well-being is an implicit goal in almost all of those. People want better housing and transit so they can live happier lives. They want to be safe so that the subjective quality of their lives improves. Curiously, however, well-being is often omitted from formal discussion in policy procedures. It is everywhere and nowhere at the same time: It forms the backbone of almost every policy aim and yet is less often pursued in its own right.

Why is that? We suspect it is because the brass-tacks issues have measurable outcomes—and policymakers perceive that “well-being” is too ephemeral to be measured.

That’s where psychologists, and perhaps especially positive psychologists, can help. Well-being no longer represents an unmeasurable ephemeral concept. The field has produced and refined legitimate scientific tools. Indeed, when we started in psychology, measures of personality and many other variables were well-established, but measures of well-being were treated with some suspicion. Since then, many studies have supported the value of well-being measures.

As a result, one way we as psychologists can improve public policy is to consistently remind policymakers that well-being can be measured just like housing costs or educational tests scores. Well-being measurement is not some elusive Platonic ideal—we can find well-validated tools that assess which factors facilitate flourishing along many dimensions, including hedonic, eudaimonic, physical health, and generic happiness (for a review of some, see our 2016 overview).

Thus, when policymakers turn to the academy for recommendations, we can put front and center our history of measurement of well-being. When studying the impact of a training program in a shelter for people who lack housing, psychological well-being of those receiving the treatment can be measured rather than measuring only items designed to facilitate well-being. Current public policy issues are often framed in well-being terms—and we have tools needed to provide policy recommendations. From the effects of artificial intelligence to social media usage, an array of studies exist showing the validity of our well-being tools in aiding policymakers.

One of us has often asked students to guess which psychological variables are most strongly associated with psychological well-being. None of the students have ever guessed “generalized trust,” even though trust consistently predicts well-being, with effects as large as many more widely known measures.

Indeed, generalized trust receives limited attention among academics (for exceptions, see some of the World Happiness Reports). Policymakers, too, often underestimate the importance of trust, so one way to influence policy is to remind policymakers of the importance of building trust in order to enable flourishing. Both general trust (e.g., “Do you think most people would return money to the owner if they found a wallet containing $200?”) and institutional trust (e.g., “Do you think the government can be trusted?” “Do you think corporations are corrupt?”) have surprisingly strong relations with well-being. Trust facilitates community, relations with neighbors, and conversations with strangers.

Misperceptions often create mistrust. For example, most people underestimate the proportion of others who act in trustworthy ways, as when most people underestimate how many individuals will return money found in lost wallets. Policymakers would be well-served to understand the difference between mistrust based on false perceptions and that which is at least partly justified, and psychologists are well-placed to help with that. Highlighting the trust findings can help policymakers focus on policies most likely to matter.

Sometimes those policies can focus on correcting misperceptions. Consider, though, what hurts trust among people. Mistrust can emerge when publicized incidents provoke fear; for example, if public spaces become truly more dangerous, then trust will decline.

Positive psychologists study three main topics: positive emotional states (i.e., well-being), positive traits (i.e., virtue and character), and positive institutions. Remember the third. Work with institutions. They help define your society.

In our graduate studies, we received no training on collaborating with public institutions. A few strategies have helped us greatly:

Their guide suggests, for example, that elected leaders and government administrators often won’t read even short written summaries of policy-relevant research that academics provide. However, those same leaders might:

Initially, that sounded nonsensical to us, and disappointing after our many hours writing brief engaging summaries of research! Now, these recommendations are in accord with our observations. These interactions matter.

We’ve also learned that government-funded institutions often have limited education budgets for their staff but want to do training. If you gain respect, they may be open to you providing training to their leaders. If you don’t present your conclusions, others, who might lack a scientific foundation, will present theirs.

You can proceed with the confidence earned by well-validated science, but also mention qualifications or uncertainty. Policymakers often prefer simple answers, so social pressure discourages intellectual humility. Don’t let that preference for simplicity capture your thinking. We may be trusted more in the long run by presenting our data while admitting uncertainties or exceptions.

Let’s return to a medical metaphor. In medicine, if a prostate cancer test correctly identified 90% of men who have prostate cancer, but only 2% of men had prostate cancer, then the odds are that many positives would be false positives; in fact, most positives would probably be false positives.

That potential error does not disqualify the test—but ignoring the error would have bad consequences for everyone. Likewise, if our measures of well-being or measures of ill-being become widely used to screen students for further attention, we could recommend a test confidently and yet also need to continually remind users of the frequency of errors. Overdiagnosis could change student perceptions in unhealthy ways. Neglecting to emphasize the errors could harm people and undermine our credibility.

Adopt a strategy of confidence in the science while providing frequent reminders of necessary qualifications.

Roger G. Tweed, Ph.D., is an instructor in psychology at Douglas College.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Go to britishairways.com, log into (or create) your Executive Club account, and run an Avios award search for the same route and dates. You should see the American Airlines flight(s) appear at 7,500 Avios + a small tax amount — typically $5–$15. If the flight shows up here, you're ready to book.

Once you've confirmed availability, it's time to transfer. Here's what to do based on your points currency:

Important: Only transfer what you need. Points transferred to British Airways cannot be moved back.

Return to BA's award search (refresh if needed), select your American Airlines flight, and complete the booking. You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

Let's make this concrete. It's mid-October and you want to visit a college friend in Boston for the weekend — flying out of New York's JFK on a Friday evening, returning Sunday afternoon.

You pull up Google Flights. Friday evening nonstops from JFK to BOS? The cheapest is $189. The convenient 6:30 PM departure on American Airlines is $229. Sunday afternoon return is another $199. Round-trip cash cost: $428.

You check aa.com and confirm both flights show saver-level award availability. You open British Airways' site and find:

You transfer 15,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways — it arrives instantly. You book both flights through BA, receive your AA confirmation numbers, and log into aa.com to select your seats.

If those flights had crept up to $300 each (not unusual around Columbus Day weekend), you'd be looking at 4 cents per point — outstanding for a domestic economy booking.

You're on a standard American Airlines narrow-body — likely a Boeing 737 or Airbus A319. It's economy, which for a 45-minute flight is entirely appropriate. You'll get a beverage service, overhead bin space, and you land at the same gate, use the same terminal, and have the same on-time performance as any other passenger on that plane. The difference is that they paid $229 and you paid $5.60 plus some points that cost you roughly $150 to earn through everyday spending.

That's the FI mindset applied to travel: same experience, radically different cost.

Do This: Book Up to 355 Days Out for Holiday Travel BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance, and American releases its best saver space early. If you're targeting Thanksgiving weekend, Christmas, or a peak summer Friday, set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Award seats on popular routes at peak times go fast.

Do This: Use the Open-Jaw Rule Creatively BA allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. If you're flying into NYC but want to return from a different airport — say JFK inbound and EWR outbound — you may be able to structure this as a single open-jaw award rather than two separate bookings. Worth exploring for multi-city weekend trips.

Avoid This: Booking BA-Operated Flights with This Strategy This cannot be overstated — BA's own flights carry $300–800+ in carrier-imposed surcharges. If you accidentally book a British Airways codeshare or BA-metal flight instead of an American Airlines-operated flight, you'll owe hundreds in fees. Always verify the operating carrier before confirming. Look for 'Operated by American Airlines' in the booking details.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability Points transferred to British Airways are one-way and permanent. Never transfer until you have eyes on the specific flight, date, and saver availability you want. The 30-second search on BA's site before transferring is non-negotiable.

Do This: Keep Your Account Active Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you accumulate Avios for a future trip, make sure to earn or redeem at least a small amount every three years. Even a small shopping portal purchase through the BA Executive Club keeps your balance alive.

Do This: Stack with Other Short Hops Think about recurring trips in your life — quarterly visits to family, annual conferences, weekend trips to a nearby city. This sweet spot isn't just for one redemption; it's a repeatable system. A modest Avios balance of 30,000–45,000 points could cover three to six regional roundtrips per year.
