Why distance-based pricing changes the domestic flying equation

Most U.S. airline loyalty programs use region-based or dynamic pricing for award flights, charging the same number of miles whether you fly 200 miles or 2,000. British Airways uses distance-based pricing instead, which means shorter flights cost dramatically fewer Avios. Since BA is a Oneworld partner with American Airlines, you can use Avios to book AA-operated nonstop domestic flights. The result: a flight that AA might price at 12,500-25,000 miles can be booked for just 7,500 Avios through BA. This is one of the most reliable and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sign up for a free BA Executive Club account at ba.com. This is where your Avios balance lives and where you will search and book award flights on American Airlines.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant. Only transfer what you need for a specific booking.

On the BA website, search for your route using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for American Airlines-operated nonstop flights. Filter results to find flights coded as AA with available Avios seats.

Confirm the flight is pricing at 7,500 Avios (under 1,151 miles) or 10,000 Avios (1,151-2,000 miles). Check that taxes and fees are the expected $5.60. If prices seem high, try different dates or check that you selected a nonstop flight.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Flights under 1,151 miles cost 7,500 Avios each way in economy. Flights between 1,151-2,000 miles cost 10,000 Avios. Flights between 2,001-3,000 miles cost 12,500 Avios. The value proposition is strongest on the shortest flights where the Avios cost is lowest.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to British Airways Avios. Transfer ratios are 1:1 from Chase, Amex, and Capital One. Transfers are typically instant or within 24 hours.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. The hardest part of most award bookings is finding available seats and navigating confusing partner systems. This one simplifies both: you're searching a major U.S. airline's (AA) domestic saver inventory, which is widely available on popular short-haul routes year-round. You're not hunting for a specific aircraft with lie-flat seats or hoping a single partner releases one business class seat. Domestic economy saver space is genuinely accessible. The booking process itself is two websites: aa.com to check availability, britishairways.com to book. Neither requires a phone call, neither has complicated routing rules for simple one-way or round-trip domestic bookings, and the transfer from Chase or Amex is instant. **The three things to get right:** 1. **Confirm saver availability on AA before transferring** — This habit protects you from the only real risk (irreversible point transfers). 2. **Verify the operating carrier is American Airlines, not British Airways** — One glance at 'Operated by' in the booking details handles this. 3. **Keep your BA Executive Club account active** — Set a reminder to log in or earn at least once every 36 months so your Avios don't expire. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

Using British Airways Avios for short domestic nonstop flights on American Airlines is one of the most practical and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards. At just 7,500 Avios each way with $5.60 in fees, it dramatically undercuts what AA charges through its own program. With four major transfer partners feeding BA Avios, this sweet spot is accessible from virtually any points-earning strategy. Whether you are booking a quick NYC-Chicago hop or an LA-San Francisco shuttle, BA Avios should be your first look for short-haul domestic flights.

Our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in contemplating the nature of creativity. “You open your safe and find ashes.”

Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

C.S. Lewis (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir Surprised by Joy (public library).

With an eye to the ideal structure of the creative life, he writes:

It is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration.

This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”:

Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise.

Shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there.

Couple with John Steinbeck on the art of receiving, then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longing.

#9377. Your Prototype Is Not Being Honest With Your Users (And Here’s How To Fix It)

Eric is a Creative Technologist at ProtoPie, where he pushes the boundaries of no-code prototyping. With a background in FinTech UX design, he brings firsthand … More about Eric ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at ProtoPie who help users turn their ideas into highly interactive animations and prototypes for mobile, desktop, web, and IoT. Thank you!

There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness.

In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance users are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

Preview both fields: username shows text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

Add a new scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

Select Log In, add a Tap trigger, set response to Jump, target your dashboard scene, transition Slide in from right to left.

Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

At the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:

Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:

Move the Jump response inside this condition. Wrong credentials, empty fields, wrong format: none get through. Participants now have to actually log in. That single constraint changes the texture of every test session that follows.

Find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

This is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

This tutorial is part of the FinTech Prototyping with ProtoPie series on the ProtoPie blog. The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.

#9376. How Ideas of Masculinity Might Affect a Country’s Well-Being

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

The Internet has been awash in commentary in recent years on the topic of masculinity. It’s spawned an influx of podcasts and social media influencers—often referred to as the “manosphere”—that have attempted to define modern-day masculinity. The Netflix documentary Inside the Manosphere, hosted by British journalist and documentarian Louis Theroux, further ignited conversations as he unpacked the impact of manosphere influencers and their potentially harmful ideologies on young boys and men.

In the field of psychology, one way of thinking about masculinity is the notion of precarious manhood. As researchers Joseph Vandello and Jennifer Bosson explain, precarious manhood has three basic tenets: First, that manhood is an “elusive, achieved status, or one that must be earned”; second, that once achieved, this manhood status can be easily lost; and, third, that manhood is largely validated by others and requires demonstrations of proof.

This may align with much of the messaging in the “manosphere,” and debates about it often consider the impact on individual boys and young men. But what’s the broader impact on society? New research suggests that countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs fare worse in terms of their economies, health, and well-being.

A recent study published in Social Science & Medicine used data from the 2024 World Happiness Report (collected between 2021 and 2023), as well as data from an investigation of gender beliefs (over 33,000 college students across 62 countries from 2018 to 2020). The study’s authors, Boston College professor James Mahalik and Ph.D. candidate Michael Harris, focused on the 59 countries covered by both studies.

Precarious manhood was examined by asking respondents things like how easy it is for one to lose his status as a man and whether some boys never become men no matter how old they get. Happiness in the World Happiness Report surveys is based on the Cantril ladder: Respondents imagine a ladder, numbered from zero (the worst possible life) to 10 (the best possible life), and indicate where they personally feel like they stand on the ladder.

The researchers found that people living in countries with higher average precarious manhood beliefs tend to be less happy, while countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs tend to be happier. Lebanon and Nigeria are among the countries that have high precarious manhood beliefs and therefore low happiness. A number of Nordic countries, including Denmark, Finland, and Sweden, have low beliefs in precarious manhood and therefore high levels of happiness. The U.S. is in the mid-range for both precarious manhood beliefs and national happiness.

It may not come as a surprise to read these findings about Nordic countries, which are often categorized as more egalitarian, have more progressive gender norms, and frequently fall near the top of the World Happiness Report rankings. In the 2024 World Economic Forum Global Gender Gap Index, for example, Finland ranks no. 2 for gender parity, Sweden ranks no. 5, and Denmark ranks no. 15. Nigeria ranks no. 125 and Lebanon ranks no. 133 out of 146. The U.S. ranks no. 43. Mahalik and Harris speculate that countries with higher precarious masculine beliefs tend to be less happy because men require more validation of behaviors that emphasize domination and self-reliance.

John Helliwell, one of the founding editors of the World Happiness Report, expressed a similar sentiment. “It’s in general true that happier societies are going to be ones where groups of people don’t feel under threat or challenged,” he said. He also pointed out the social trust in Nordic countries, which has often been a distinguishing characteristic of cultures with harsher living conditions, where people are incentivized to cooperate because their survival historically depended on it.

In their recent study, Mahalik and Harris also found that countries with higher levels of precarious manhood beliefs had lower gross domestic product (GDP). They propose that in countries where masculinity is thought of as precarious, men may be discouraged from participating in fields that are critical yet perceived as feminine, like caregiving and education, and that such beliefs may also restrict women’s opportunities in the workforce—relegating women to fields considered feminine or restricting them from the workforce altogether. However, they note that lower GDP may be what fosters precarious masculine beliefs in the first place, as economic challenges could heighten fears about fulfilling the traditional masculine role of being a provider.

Other research finds different consequences for believing in this elusive and hard-earned version of masculinity. In a study of 62 countries by Vandello, Bosson, and other colleagues in 2023, they found that men in countries with higher precarious manhood beliefs had lower life expectancy by several years than men in countries with lower precarious manhood beliefs.

Why? There could be many explanations, but they also found that national precarious manhood beliefs predicted risky health behaviors, such as substance abuse, extreme sports, and reckless driving.

Mahalik, who’s been studying gender socialization since the early 1990s, said there is longstanding research around the gender socialization of girls—more specifically, the messages they receive about body image, which research has linked to eating disorders. As Mahalik told me, “I’ve been interested in examining the messages that culture also gives to men, some of which are contradictory and inconsistent, and the impact of what men take in about their external valuation of worth.”

While Mahalik’s and Harris’s study ultimately doesn’t prove that beliefs in precarious manhood cause lower national happiness, it raises important questions about the link between rigid masculinity norms and well-being. As researchers continue to examine what makes a happy nation, this new study suggests that the answer may not just lie in government policy, but in how cultures interpret and frame masculinity. As Mahalik told me, “What sort of community are we creating if culturally we’re endorsing a model of masculinity in which men have to constantly guard against losing their status as men?”

Spencer Spellman is a writer, editor, and photographer, with his writing and photography appearing in the Los Angeles Times, Condé Nast Traveler, AFAR, Sunset, Outside Magazine, Smithsonian Magazine, and Travel + Leisure.

Many decision makers are not drawing from the relevant findings in well-being research. Here's how to change that.

Several years ago, rummaging through the archives of the Academy of American Poets, I came upon a box labeled “Ballots 1950” — the record of the secret vote by the chancellors the year the Academy’s prestigious fellowship was awarded to E.E. Cummings, catapulting him into renown. The voting process is a black box — no one outside the Academy ever finds out who else is in the running and by how much the winner wins.

Leafing through the ballots, one other name appeared over and over, so much so that I was impelled to count.

Marianne Moore had lost by one vote, never knowing how close she had come. It would be many more years until, at 77, she was finally awarded the fellowship.

Long before that, before she won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award (sharing a table with Rachel Carson at the ceremony), Moore had set down her views on writing in a series of essays later collected in the out-of-print gem Predilections (public library). Pulsating through them is a reckoning with the impossible task of the writer — to weave tapestries of truth and meaning from the tenuous thread of words on the ramshackle loom of language.

In an essay titled “Feeling and Precision,” Moore writes:

Feeling at its deepest — as we all have reason to know — tends to be inarticulable. If it does manage to be articulate, it is likely to seem overcondensed, so that the author is resisted as being enigmatic or disobliging or arrogant.

How we name what we feel is not so much a matter of our writing style as of our style of being, because in order to articulate something we must first apprehend it and we apprehend every smallest thing with the whole person — with the frame of reference that is our entire life, the sum of our experience and memory. When “one of New York’s more painstaking magazines” asked Moore to distill her poetic style into a formula, she fought back the “dictatorial” reflex to quip:

You don’t devise a rhythm, the rhythm is the person, and the sentence but a radiograph of the personality.

And yet a personality can write with more or less persuasion — that is, write more or less well — depending on what the person brings to the writing. In another essay from the collection, Moore identifies the three psychological elements necessary for persuasive writing: “humility, concentration, and gusto.” A generation after Mark Twain assured his friend Helen Keller when she was accused of plagiarism that “substantially all ideas are second-hand, consciously and unconsciously drawn from a million outside sources,” she writes:

Humility… is armor, for it realizes that it is impossible to be original, in the sense of doing something that has never been thought of before. Originality is in any case a by-product of sincerity; that is to say, of feeling that is honest and accordingly rejects anything that might cloud the impression.

By “concentration” Moore means a kind of discipline — annealing the essence of the sentiment by cutting away all superfluous explanations, elaborations, and distractions of stylistic posturing, being maximally truthfully in the most minimal way possible. Observing that there is always a “helpless sincerity which precipitates a poem” and that a good poem is always “a concentrate,” she writes:

Concentration — indispensable to persuasion — may feel to itself crystal clear, yet be through its very compression the opposite… I myself would rather be told too little than too much.

Long before we had the language of extrinsic and intrinsic motivation, of finite and infinite games, Moore uses a lovely word, now dusty, for that peculiar private zeal propelling all creative work with its twin dynamos of discipline and deliverance: “gusto.” Echoing Rachel Carson’s abiding advice on writing — “If you write what you yourself sincerely think and feel and are interested in,” she had counseled a young writer, “the chances are very high that you will interest other people as well.” — Moore offers:

Gusto thrives on freedom, and freedom in art, as in life, is the result of a discipline imposed by ourselves. Moreover, any writer overwhelmingly honest about pleasing himself is almost sure to please others.

She maps the fundamental relationship between the three:

Humility is an indispensable teacher, enabling concentration to heighten gusto.

When creating in integrity with these three values, it ceases to matter how the work is received because the process of locating and articulating the truth as you feel it, the world as you see it, is its own reward. In what may be the best advice I have encountered on how to orient to your own work, Moore writes:

There are always objecters, but we must not be sensitive about not being liked or not being printed… The thing is to see the vision and not deny it; or care and admit that we do.

Complement with Walt Whitman on how to keep criticism from sinking your soul and Mary Oliver’s advice on writing, then savor the moving story of how Marianne Moore saved a rare tree with a poem.

#9374. Algorithmic Theming Engines: Building Self-Correcting Color Systems With `contrast-color()`

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The HTTP Archive Web Almanac has been tracking color contrast failures for years. The numbers have barely moved. After half a decade of design system tooling, accessibility linters, and entire JavaScript libraries dedicated to computing readable text colors, 70% of websites still fail basic WCAG contrast checks in 2025. The WebAIM Million paints an even grimmer picture — 83.9% of homepages flagged for low contrast text in 2026, up from 79.1% in 2025. The rate improves by maybe a few percentage points per year on one benchmark and actually gets worse on another. That’s not progress — that’s proof that relying on runtime JavaScript for something this fundamental doesn’t scale across the open web. We didn’t need better libraries. We’ve needed better CSS.

The contrast-color() function is that better CSS. One declaration. The browser runs the contrast math during style computation, before the page paints, and hands you the right text color. No library, no build step, no hydration flash.

Note: If you’ve seen it called color-contrast() in older articles and spec drafts — that name was changed, and the old syntax no longer works in any browser.

The Level 5 version is simple. You give it a color. It gives you back black or white, whichever has more contrast against your input.

Change --brand-color to neon green, text goes black. Change it to midnight navy, text goes white. Swap themes at runtime via JavaScript and the text adapts instantly — no event listeners, no recalculation.

A few things to know about the current version:

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

This function lives across two specifications. That’s unusual and worth understanding.

CSS Color Level 5 defines what browsers ship today. One color in, black or white out. The algorithm is deliberately marked “UA-defined”, meaning the browser decides what math to use internally. Right now, every engine uses WCAG 2.x relative luminance. But that “UA-defined” label isn’t accidental — it’s a planned escape hatch.

You’ll see APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) mentioned a lot in this context. APCA models how human eyes actually perceive contrast, factoring in font weight, spatial frequency, and ambient light — a genuine improvement over the WCAG 2.x formula. By not locking “use WCAG 2.x” into the Level 5 spec, browser vendors could swap to APCA later without breaking any existing code. If the spec had shipped with a wcag2() keyword as the default, every site using it would’ve been stuck on the old math permanently.

But APCA’s future is far less certain than the hype suggests. Adrian Roselli’s “WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026” lays out the current situation clearly: APCA was pulled from the WCAG 3 working draft in mid-2023 after failing to gain enough Working Group support. The WCAG 3 spec currently says the contrast algorithm is “yet to be determined,” and the standard itself may not be finalized until 2030 or later. Roselli also filed a Chromium issue in May 2024 asking for the “Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm” experiment flag to be removed from DevTools entirely, arguing that the implementation is outdated and risks misleading developers into thinking APCA is further along — or more official — than it actually is. That issue is still open.

None of this means APCA is dead. The research behind it is peer-reviewed and substantive, and its creator has noted that colors passing APCA guidelines greatly exceed WCAG 2 minimums in the vast majority of cases. But right now, there is no guarantee APCA will be the algorithm that replaces WCAG 2.x — and that uncertainty matters for contrast-color(). If a different algorithm wins out, or if WCAG 3 adopts something entirely new, the “UA-defined” label means browsers can adapt without breaking your code. It also means the Level 6 features — candidate color lists, target ratios, the tbd-fg/tbd-bg keywords — are all designed around an algorithm that may or may not materialize in its current form.

CSS Color Level 6 adds the extended syntax — candidate color lists and target contrast ratios:

The browser would evaluate each candidate left to right and pick the first that meets the 4.5:1 AA threshold. The tbd-fg and tbd-bg keywords indicate whether the base color is foreground or background, which matters for directional contrast models like APCA. This is all Working Draft territory — doubly so given APCA’s uncertain status. Use the Level 5 version for now.

This one’s in better shape than most new CSS features. All three major engines have shipped it in stable releases: Chrome 147 (April 2026), Firefox 146, and Safari 26.0. It reached Baseline Newly Available status in April 2026. Check caniuse for the full version matrix. All three engines pass the Web Platform Tests for contrast-color(), which means the edge cases (e.g., tie-breaking logic, color space conversion, syntax parsing) behave the same across browsers.

The raw global support percentage on caniuse looks low, but that mostly reflects enterprise browsers and people who never update. If you’re reading this, your browser almost certainly supports it already.

Progressive enhancement is straightforward using @supports:

Older browsers get white text with a dark shadow for legibility. Supporting browsers get the native calculation. Nobody sees broken text.

One thing to watch for: automated accessibility scanners (Lighthouse, Axe, etc.) can’t evaluate text-shadow. They only look at the computed color against background-color. So the fallback will still get flagged as a contrast failure in CI/CD pipelines, even if the shadow makes the text perfectly legible to human eyes. If your team runs automated a11y checks, you may need to allowlist that specific rule or add a comment explaining why the flag is a false positive.

This can trip people up: “I used the contrast function, so my site passes accessibility checks now, right?”

Mathematically? Usually yes. There is a persistent myth that for certain “mid-tone” backgrounds, both black and white fail the standard WCAG 4.5:1 AA ratio. That’s mathematically false. Under the WCAG 2.x relative luminance formula, there is absolutely no background color where both pure black and pure white fail AA. One (or both) will always pass.

Take #2277d3 (a medium blue). It sits right on a mathematical knife-edge where both black and white actually pass AA (both hit roughly 4.58:1). contrast-color() will hand you whichever has the slight mathematical edge.

But here is the actual gotcha: the WCAG 2.x math has known perceptual blind spots. That same #2277d3 with black text mathematically passes AA, but to human eyes, it can be incredibly difficult to read. contrast-color() gives you mathematical compliance, which is great for automated audits, but that doesn’t always equal perceptual accessibility. (This is exactly why APCA exists and why the spec was designed to let browsers swap algorithms later.)

Furthermore, if you’re aiming for the stricter WCAG AAA standard (7.0:1), a true dead zone does exist. For backgrounds with a luminance between roughly 10% and 30%, neither black nor white will hit 7:1. In those cases, contrast-color() can’t save you — it just hands you the “least bad” failing option.

If you’re animating a background from white to black on hover:

The background fades smoothly over one second. But because the Level 5 output is a discrete value (black or white), the text color can’t be interpolated. It snaps.

And here is the visual gotcha: the snap doesn’t happen halfway through. If you’ve been building themes for a while, you probably have muscle memory from the old Sass days, where we checked if lightness($bg) > 50%. That relied on HSL lightness, where 50% is the geometric midpoint.

But WCAG 2.x relative luminance is a non-linear scale. Under the WCAG formula, the mathematical tipping point — where black and white have identical contrast against the background — actually occurs at approximately 18% relative luminance (specifically ~17.9%).

Because of that, the visual behavior during a white-to-black fade is heavily skewed. The text doesn’t snap in the middle. It stays black for the vast majority of the animation, only snapping to white at the very tail-end of the transition when the background gets extremely dark. It’s a jarring, late hard cut.

You might assume transition-behavior: allow-discrete fixes this. It doesn’t. allow-discrete does not fix the jarring visual experience because it cannot interpolate a binary output; it only shifts the timing of the hard snap to the 50% mark of the animation duration. If you need smooth text color transitions, you’ll have to layer color-mix() or manage the crossfade yourself.

If the background is a perfect middle gray where both black and white produce identical contrast ratios, the spec has a hardcoded tiebreaker: white wins. Not a big deal in practice, but worth knowing if you’re debugging gray palettes and the text isn’t doing what you expect.

The function takes a flat value. You can’t pass it a gradient or a url(). contrast-color(linear-gradient(...)) is a parse error. If your background is a photo or a complex gradient, you still need JavaScript or manually color-pick for overlay text.

Pass a semi-transparent color, and the browser blends it against an assumed opaque canvas (usually white) before running the contrast math. It’s not ignoring your alpha channel — it’s compositing it. But the result might surprise you if you expected the function to “see through” to whatever’s actually behind the element.

If a user enables Windows High Contrast, the forced-colors: active media query kicks in and the browser aggressively overwrites author-defined colors. contrast-color() bows out — forced system colors like CanvasText take over completely. You don’t need to write manual media queries to undo your contrast logic; the browser handles the hierarchy.

Black or white sounds limiting, but once you feed that output into other CSS color functions, you can build an entire component palette off a single custom property.

Pure black text on a vibrant card looks fine. Pure white on a coral card can feel flat. What if the contrast text was a very dark or very light tint of the background color instead?

Kevin Hamer explored related territory in his CSS-Tricks piece “Approximating contrast-color() With Other CSS Features”, where he used OKLCH lightness and round() to approximate the black/white switch without contrast-color() — essentially oklch(from round(1.21 - l) 0 0). That’s a polyfill strategy: get the binary light/dark decision working in browsers that don’t support the native function yet. What we’re doing here is different — we start with contrast-color()’s native output and then enrich it by injecting the background’s own hue:

When contrast-color() returns white, l is 1 (full lightness). When it returns black, l is 0. By pulling the background’s hue back in and adding a touch of chroma, you get text that reads as a deep dark indigo or a pale icy indigo instead of generic black/white. Hamer’s approach gives you the black/white decision without browser support; this one takes the decision the browser already made and gives it personality.

Fair warning: By tweaking the lightness and chroma of the black/white output, you can push a borderline contrast ratio into failing territory. Always run your tinted output through an accessibility linter before shipping.

Also worth noting: This example chains two very modern features — contrast-color() and oklch(from ...). If either one isn’t supported, the entire declaration fails silently. Your @supports block needs to test for both:

Similar idea, simpler API. Mix the sharp black/white output back into the background to soften it:

One custom property driving text, border, and potentially box-shadow or outline. Change --alert-color and the entire component recalculates.

This pattern also works well for ::placeholder text, which is a common pain point in dynamic theming. Placeholder text should be readable but visually softer than the input’s main text — color-mix() with contrast-color() gets you there:

50% mix gives you a muted but legible placeholder that adapts automatically to whatever background the input sits on.

For apps that support system light/dark mode:

When the operating system switches to dark mode, --surface resolves to #121212, and contrast-color() returns white. No media queries, no JavaScript theme detection. The whole chain resolves natively.

The practical payoff: every one of these libraries existed because CSS couldn’t do contrast math. If you’re only using them for readable-text-color selection, you can pull them out of your runtime entirely:

You might still need these for generating complex color scales, but the contrast-for-readability use case is now covered natively.

Beyond bundle size, there’s a performance angle that’s easy to overlook. Those JavaScript libraries don’t just cost you network bytes — they run on the main thread. Every time a theme changes or a component mounts with a dynamic background, your JS has to parse the color, compute luminance, decide black or white, and write the result back to the DOM. That’s main-thread work competing with layout, event handlers, and everything else your app is doing. contrast-color() moves all of that into the browser’s native style computation phase — heavily optimized C++ that runs before paint. For apps with lots of themed components, that’s a real difference in responsiveness.

There’s also a subtle bug that goes away: hydration flash. In React or Vue SSR apps, the server renders HTML without JavaScript. The client then hydrates, running JS to calculate contrast and inject the correct text color. For a brief window between initial paint and hydration, the text is either invisible or the wrong color. Moving contrast into CSS eliminates that entirely — the browser resolves the correct color during the initial paint, before JavaScript loads.

Sass era. You’d write a function that checked lightness($bg) > 50% and returned black or white at compile time. Worked for static themes. Completely useless for user-picked colors, CMS palettes, or dark mode, because the output was baked into the CSS file and could never change at runtime.

The variable toggle hack. When CSS custom properties shipped, people got creative. GitHub used a version of this for their issue label picker — splitting colors into --r, --g, --b channels, calculating Rec.709 luminance inside calc(), multiplying by negative infinity, and clamping to 0 or 1. It worked. It was also unreadable, unmaintainable, and would break silently if you got one parenthesis wrong. (Kevin Hamer’s OKLCH-based approximation is the most elegant version of this lineage — cleaner math, better perceptual alignment — but it’s still a workaround for a function that now ships natively.)

contrast-color() replaces all of these approaches with a single function call. And because the spec lets browsers upgrade the underlying algorithm, your code won’t need to change if and when a successor to WCAG 2.x contrast math lands — whether that’s APCA or something else entirely.

That 70% failure rate was never about developers refusing to care about contrast. It was about the distance between caring and shipping — the library, the build step, the runtime calculation, the hydration flash, the one component someone forgot to wire up. Every gap in that chain was a spot where accessibility quietly dropped out.

contrast-color() doesn’t make developers care more. It makes caring cost nothing.

#9373. How Paternity Leave Policies Help Moms, Babies, and Families

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work.

I’m a certified family life educator, and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work. So I was aware of the benefits his leave could have for our family—in theory.

Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community.

During his leave time, my spouse took our oldest child to playdates and birthday parties. He quickly became connected with our small-town network of families with kids close in age. I witnessed my spouse becoming more comfortable being the “main” parent in public, going to kid-centered community events, and connecting with other parents.

Our family is still seeing the benefits of those few weeks 10 years later.

Leave for supporting parents after the birth of a child isn’t standardized or required by law in most places in the U.S. Even countries with generous paid time off for the birthing parent don’t always offer similarly generous time for the non-birthing parent.

This diversity in leave policies can make it hard to assess the impact of leave for the non-birthing parent. But existing research suggests that extended leave for birthing parents and moderate leave for non-birthing partners positively impact infant well-being and reduce postpartum mental health challenges.

Leave for both parents with the birth of a child can significantly benefit parental mental health overall and maternal mental health specifically. Paternity leave assists in the mother’s recovery and contributes to less of an increase in stress and depression than for mothers whose partners didn’t take leave.

One Swedish study showed that flexibility within paternal leave policies, such as allowing new dads to take intermittent time off after the birth of a child, helped reduce the incidence of maternal postpartum health complications.

Children also benefit from paternity leave. When a father takes significant leave—meaning at least two weeks—children report experiencing more father-child closeness and better communication in the relationship up to nine years later. And overall child health tends to improve when fathers take paternity leave.

When paid leave policies are available for both mothers and fathers, breastfeeding is more likely to last longer. Longer breastfeeding is strongly linked to overall infant health and decreased infant mortality.

Allowing both parents to have sufficient time off to bond and adjust to their new roles can also have longer-term benefits within the family unit and contribute toward more equity in child rearing. Even in 2026, mothers are often considered the “default” parent, with fathers taking a more secondary role.

While fathers are more involved now than in previous generations, mothers are still more likely to be the first call from school. And even with an involved father, mothers continue to carry the invisible mental load of the family, an unseen burden of data, obligations, and preemptive planning tasks. This overreliance on mothers comes with a price: Mothers report being more stressed and tired than fathers do.

As I experienced in my own family, when fathers have ample time off, it sets up the dynamic to be more balanced between parents. This helps reduce the strain on recovering mothers and redistributes some of the care work that goes into raising children.

What’s more, paid leave policies have been shown to help families’ financial health. Pay rates during leave can vary widely depending on your company, organization, or country. Without full or close to full pay, many families cannot afford to take leave.

In the U.S., for example, the Family and Medical Leave Act allows time off, but not in all circumstances, nor is that time required to be paid. Many families cannot afford to take the full allowable time off, using up sick or vacation time if available. Many parents in the U.S. end up going back to work sooner than seems healthy.

New parents in the U.S. often find themselves in an economic bind—they can’t afford to take leave, nor can they afford to rely on a single income to have a parent stay home. But many also can’t afford the child care rates for newborns, which tend to be particularly high. National averages for infant care at child care centers are nearly $200 more per month than toddler care. While rates vary significantly depending on where you live and what type of care you choose, infant care remains the most expensive.

Despite the lack of a paid U.S. federal leave policy for parents, both domestic and multinational companies have noticed that their workers care about parental leave policies. Some have begun to offer leave for supporting parents in order to recruit and retain workers.

U.S. leave policies consistently rank at or near the bottom when compared with other similarly developed countries, like the 38 members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

Some countries follow a “use-it-or-lose-it” model of parental leave, where fathers in particular are encouraged to take a more substantial role in child care. Sweden and Norway, for example, earmark 90 days of leave for each parent, and it cannot be transferred to or split with the other parent. This encourages both parents to take time off.

There are many options across countries with parental leave policies. Flexibility and defined expectations seem to be key contributors to getting the most out of the parental leave that is offered.

When non-birthing parents are men, another barrier to taking leave is the perceived social acceptability within their communities. Even when paid paternity leave is available, many men struggle to take it because of how traditional gender roles and expectations of masculinity frame child care as women’s work.

To offset these kinds of social pressures, countries like Japan and Austria offer incentives such as bonus leave time for families when fathers actually take their available leave. Germany offers a similar bonus, and it has found improved couple relationship satisfaction when fathers take more of their leave time.

Beyond improvements in maternal and infant health, both parents taking leave can create a more equitable workplace environment. Disparities and discrimination that come when only women take leave after birth can lessen when fathers and other supporting parents also take leave. Childbearing women are then less likely to be penalized, formally or informally, for taking parental leave.

Paid parental leave policies that provide leave for all parents, regardless of gender, also can help reduce structural inequality in the workplace across race and class. In the U.S., Hispanic and Black workers often have less access to paid leave policies and may experience increased pressure to return to work earlier than their white counterparts.

As more states, countries, and corporations adopt more flexible and inclusive leave policies, researchers will continue to learn how parental leave benefits both parents and children. What they’ve found so far leads me to believe that, just like we’ve seen with prenatal care and early education programs, parental leave will prove to be an early investment in healthy children and families that pays dividends in the long term.

#9372. Rare Altdorfer landscape previously unknown to scholars to be auctioned next month

Albrecht Altdorfer, A thickly wooded landscape with a rainbow behind the trees and a distant outcrop to the right beneath a cloud-laden sky (around 1520)

A rare landscape by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Altdorfer will be offered at auction at Sotheby’s Old Masters Evening Sale in London on 9 December, with an estimated price of between £3m and £5m.

The painting of a thickly wooded landscape and a rainbow against a densely clouded sky, dating from around 1520, surfaced in a Swiss private collection. It was previously unknown to Altdorfer scholars and does not feature in the artist’s catalogue raisonné. It is one of only three known oil landscapes by Altdorfer, who is considered one of the first landscape artists. The other two are both in museums—one is in Munich’s Alte Pinakothek, and the other in London’s National Gallery.

“To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field,” says George Gordon, the chairman of Sotheby’s Worldwide Old Masters Department.

The current owner of the painting inherited it from his father, who purchased it in 1957 from the collection of a noble Austrian family, the House of Harrach. Painted on parchment, it was later glued to a wooden panel support. It is the smallest of Altdorfer’s known landscapes. A distant castle perches on a rocky outcrop beyond the rain-wettened forest and undergrowth that dominates the painting, which is signed.

Altdorfer was born in 1480 in Regensburg in southern Germany, spent most of his career there, also working as a politician, and died in the city in 1538. His densely wooded landscapes are drawn from the mixed deciduous and evergreen forests either side of the Danube downstream from Regensburg, Gordon says.

He says it was difficult to give a price estimate for the painting because no Altdorfer work has been offered on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery paid the reported sum of £2.4m for Christ Taking Leave of His Mother (around 1520). It was one of the highest prices ever paid for a work of art at that time.

“We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon says. “It could fetch more than our estimate. I think it’s quite likely that museums will be interested.”

Sotheby’s will exhibit the painting in New York from 7-19 November and in London from 4-9 December.

#9371. The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI

“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.

Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

In her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies, Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech.) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:

Our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.

Comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

That’s exactly what our monthly wallpapers series has been all about for over 15 years now. It’s a chance to step away from the everyday and dive into a fun, creative project. And this month is no different!

Three years after he became the second-youngest laureate of the Nobel Prize, awarded him for literature that “with clear-sighted earnestness illuminates the problems of the human conscience,” Albert Camus (November 7, 1913–January 4, 1960) died in a car crash with an unused train ticket to the same destination in his pocket. The writings he left behind — about the key to strength of character, about creativity as resistance, about the antidotes to the absurdity of life, about happiness as our moral obligation — endure as a living testament to Mary Shelley’s conviction that “it is by words that the world’s great fight, now in these civilized times, is carried on.”

Camus addressed his views on writing most directly in a 1943 essay about the novel, included in his altogether indispensable Lyrical and Critical Essays (public library).

One must be two persons when one writes… The great problem is to translate what one feels into what one wants others to feel. We call a writer bad when he expresses himself in reference to an inner context the reader cannot know. The mediocre writer is thus led to say anything he pleases.

In a sentiment James Baldwin would echo in his advice on writing, insisting that “beyond talent lie all the usual words: discipline, love, luck, but most of all, endurance,” Camus observes that all creative endeavor demands of us “a certain constancy of soul, and a human and literary knowledge of sacrifice.” He writes:

To someone who asked Newton how he had managed to construct his theory, he could reply: “By thinking about it all the time.” There is no greatness without a little stubbornness.

Nearly a century after Tchaikovsky asserted that “a self-respecting artist must not fold his hands on the pretext that he is not in the mood,” Camus adds:

Great novels… prove the effectiveness of human creation. They convince one that the work of art is a human thing, never human enough, and that its creator can do without dictates from above. Works of art are not born in flashes of inspiration but in a daily fidelity.

Complement with more excellent advice on writing from Mary Oliver, Rachel Carson, Maya Angelou, George Saunders, John Steinbeck, and Ernest Hemingway, then revisit the beautiful letter of gratitude Camus sent to his childhood teacher shortly after receiving the Nobel Prize.

#9368. How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When educators feel emotionally and physically supported, they’re in a much better position to support their students. In India, where the relationship between teacher and student has long been central to education, caring for teachers is essential to sustaining that connection.

India’s education system comprises over 1 million government schools and more than 82,000 government-aided institutions. Serving approximately 167 million children, India administers the world’s largest education system. Increasingly, educators around the world recognize that social-emotional skills like navigating conflict and building healthy relationships are just as essential as academic learning—and India’s own national policies have begun to reflect that shift.

The 2020 National Education Policy calls social-emotional learning (SEL) “a critical aspect of any student’s holistic development.” That’s supported by the National Curriculum Framework, which recognizes the importance of fostering stronger student-teacher relationships to accomplish this approach.

Aditi Ramanthan, a high school biology teacher with almost 20 years of experience, has seen the shift toward more thoughtful discussion and implementation of SEL throughout her time teaching. However, as SEL becomes a more important part of education, the question is not only how to support students, it’s how to support the teachers who are being asked to help them develop these skills.

From this perspective, the future of teaching in India may not be defined only by new curricula or digital tools, but by whether schools can become places where the hearts of teachers are systematically cared for, so they can, in turn, care for the hearts of children.

“The primary need is psychological safety,” says Ramanathan. “Instead of constantly viewing teachers as being emotionally self-sufficient, creating a space where they can ask for help.”

In recent years, SEL implementation in India has been widely championed and led by school counselors, with educators throughout grade levels recognizing it as something that should be on par with academic curriculum.

“In India, social-emotional learning is just beginning to come into focus,” says Ramanathan. “Until recently, it wasn’t really part of mainstream conversations in schools, but now we’re starting to talk about it more seriously.”

Ramanthan argues that while SEL has become more widely accepted in recent years, it should be treated as a basic professional requirement for teachers, much like first-aid training, if it’s to be successfully implemented in schools. While schools routinely prepare educators to respond to physical emergencies, far less attention is given to the emotional crises that are likely to unfold in their classrooms. She suggests that SEL training should be universal for teachers, equipping them to understand and respond to students’ inner lives, not just their academic performance.

“We are not trained for SEL, and I wish we were,” says Ramanthan. “We’re given first aid training, but we are not given SEL training, and I think all of us should do SEL training.”

In a former position, Vrinda Loiwal, founder of the Center for Social Emotional Learning, designed SEL assessments for students, primarily in government-run schools. Once every three months, she would enter classrooms across the country to see how SEL was being interpreted, taught, and assessed.

“One of the challenges to children’s well-being is that even if you teach one SEL standalone lesson once a week, it has to be embodied in the math class, and the English class, and on the playground, and in the messaging all around the students,” Loiwal says. “I believe that there’s very little impact that can come with just a standalone lesson.”

Inconsistency is another challenge. Loiwal explains that about a decade ago, the Delhi school district adopted a new SEL program—and after years of teacher training and evaluation, they had evidence that what they were doing was working. However, in recent years with a new government in place, the program was scrapped and replaced.

While on paper these new policies tick all the boxes for SEL implementation, when it comes to policy, introducing new required methods every few years disrupts the system just as educators begin to find their footing. They are constantly forced to recalibrate their entire approach, which creates an immense amount of pressure on the educators who are already overwhelmed and stretched thin for time.

“All the teacher training now has to happen all over again and in a slightly new way because now there’s a new curriculum,” says Loiwal. “We all agree that you have to teach addition and subtraction in math, but we don’t yet all agree that we have to teach SEL skills or build SEL cultures. These are early efforts, and they’re building. Then the politics change and it feels like two steps forward, one step back.”

At the Kaveri Group of Institutes in Pune—which includes schools that range from elementary to graduate level—leaders see the strain up close. Teachers are being asked to carry the weight of being disciplinarians, counselors, curriculum experts, and cultural bridges with no real pause in the day to breathe or reflect.

“An educator is expected to teach, educate, to discipline, to mold the child, to develop the child, to understand the parents, different stakeholders, all of that,” says Deepa Kajale, a consultant for Kaveri. “It’s really overwhelming for the educator to put up with all these kinds of responsibilities.”

Kajale is a play- and arts-based therapist and school psychologist who has worked with many interventions and iterations of SEL frameworks to foster inclusive, emotionally safe environments. While policymakers are increasingly viewing SEL as essential and not optional, Kajale and her colleagues at Kaveri are attempting to bridge the gap between newly required written frameworks and implementation.

For example, at the Kaveri Gifted Education and Research Center—which aims to identify and nurture gifted students across India—school counselors offer confidential spaces for teachers to talk about both professional and personal struggles like burnout and family stress, and they encourage educators to speak with counselors as a form of ongoing support, rather than viewing reaching out as a last resort.

Devasena Desai, Associate Director for Kaveri Counseling, Empowerment and Gifted Unit since 2014, says that in addition to offering wellness sessions where they talk about nutrition and menopause, they also celebrate Teacher’s Day. Each year on September 5, they host a large gathering complete with awards to teachers for creativity and innovation, live music, and loud cheering as colleagues are honored.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world

Additionally, she says one of the most fruitful decisions they made is to offer outsourced counselors from other districts for their educators to speak to.

“Because sometimes you don’t want to talk to the person whom you bump into every day,” says Desai. “Maybe you’re not comfortable and we want to respect that. There are people who wouldn’t mind and there are some people who wouldn’t want to, so that option is there.”

Along with this more formal support, Kaveri has built in daily rituals of connection, including listening circles where they talk about how to manage varying responsibilities, as well as more sensitive topics like overload and grief.

“What we have introduced in the last two years is talking about trauma, talking about grief, talking about single parenting, blended families, and how to embrace that,” says Desai.

According to a paper published in June of this year that studied SEL in Nagaland, India, successful implementation requires specific teacher and parent engagement as well as dedicated training and resources. Additionally, SEL had to be contextually adapted and culturally aligned with local traditions.

The team at Kaveri understands the importance of cultural relevance when introducing these practices and often draw on concepts like guru and dharma to restore social meaning to the role of the teacher. The ideal of the teacher as a guru or a guide for both knowledge and character still carries significant cultural weight.

Unfortunately, that ideal can collide with the modern reality of rapid policy shifts, new technologies, and a workforce made up largely of women juggling caregiving at home and expanding expectations at work.

“Within the professional identity, there is a personal identity with roles, responsibilities, and a lot to take care of as a woman,” says Kajale. “So that adds up to the emotional exhaustion that an educator goes through.”

Guru is a Sanskrit word meaning “heavy” or “weighty,” used to describe a spiritual teacher or guide who dispels ignorance and leads a student toward self-realization. Rather than abandon the guru ideal as outdated, Kaveri is reclaiming it for the 21st century by rooting teacher support in Indian knowledge systems. In this model, SEL is not just a borrowed framework or a one-off workshop; it’s woven into listening circles, parenting programs, and grief support; and practiced by using a model of wellness that treats educators as whole human beings—body, breath, mind, and spirit.

“We believe that for the holistic development of a person, you have to be very balanced with all your koshas,” says Malati Kalmadi, secretary of Kannada Sangha Public Trust.

In the Panchakosha model from Vedantic philosophy, there are five koshas—or the “five layers of human existence”—including the Annamaya (physical), Pranamaya (energetic), Manomaya (psychological), Vigynamaya (intellectual), and Anandamaya (spiritual). This holistic journey begins with the Annamaya Kosha, focusing on our physical essence through the food we consume. Beyond the visible body lies the Pranamaya Kosha, the vital energy that governs our internal systems—respiratory, circulatory, and nervous.

Achieving equilibrium in these physical and energetic layers is the foundation for mastering the Manomaya Kosha, or the mind. The Vijnanamaya Kosha connects us to our intellect and discernment, while the Anandamaya Kosha is our innermost peace.

Unlike Western perspectives that often separate diet from cognition, the Panchakosha model believes that the food we eat deeply influences the nature of our thoughts, inextricably linking our physical choices to our emotional and mental clarity.

Parents play a vital role in supporting this intentional shift back toward traditional models; Kaveri is working to more deliberately support parents in lifting these inherent values. In addition to the Mindful Parenting Program Workbook they created in collaboration with the Greater Good Science Center’s Parenting Program, they have taken it upon themselves to create additional parenting modules to help parents address the evolving cultural landscape and shifts between millennials, Gen-Z, and Generation Alpha.

To help parents, students, and educators align their koshas, they have experts speak to them about how to switch from “fast food” to “slow food,” helping them become more conscious of what they put into their bodies. One of their team members also went to Bangalore for a training on traditional Indian well-being therapies to provide an alternative to Western medicine.

“We feel that once we are able to get all these things into place, then the wisdom and the thoughts actually move towards spirituality,” says Kalmadi. “Our aim is taking the child towards this track for a better society.”

While there is no single clean-cut path forward to create schools and districts grounded in SEL, educators across India are already showing that change is possible. By caring for teachers as whole people and drawing on both new research and longstanding cultural traditions, schools can create environments where educators feel supported to care for themselves, their students, and one another.

In that sense, the future of SEL in India may begin not with another mandate, but with a growing recognition that when we care for the people who teach, we strengthen the entire educational community.

“There is slowly a conversation happening between parents, and schools, and teachers, which earlier was not happening consciously, but now we are doing it very, very consciously,” says Kalmadi. “This is proving to be very beneficial for the entire educational ecosystem.”

Emily Brower is the Education Editor at the Greater Good Science Center and an Associate Producer of The Science of Happiness podcast. In her role as Education Editor, she has covered educator well-being around the world, exploring the experiences and challenges of educators in Ukraine, Singapore, and Spain. Previously, as a music and travel journalist, she contributed to publications including Pure Nowhere, Fifty Grande, and KCPR, covering destinations across Southern and Northern California and the Central Coast. Emily earned a B.S. in Journalism with a concentration in Public Relations and a minor in Art History from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo. She later received her master’s degree from the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism.

#9367. Guillaume Cerutti named president of the Palace of Versailles

After eight months without a president, the Palace of Versailles finally has a new leader. Guillaume Cerutti, 60, has been named the president of the prestigious institution, according to the newspaper Politico. A graduate of France’s elite École nationale d’administration (ENA) and a former senior civil servant in the finance ministry, he succeeds Christophe Leribault, who was appointed president and director of the Louvre in February following the abrupt departure of Laurence des Cars.

The appointment marks Cerutti’s return to public service after two decades in the private sector. In a twist of fate, he is following in the footsteps of his former mentor, Jean-Jacques Aillagon, who headed the Palace and National Estate of Versailles from 2007 to 2011. Cerutti worked closely with Aillagon for many years, first at the Centre Pompidou, where Aillagon was the president from 1996 to 2002, and later as his chief of staff when Aillagon became France’s culture minister in 2002. “Having worked alongside Guillaume [Cerutti] for decades, I know he has all the experience and qualities needed to lead Versailles,” Aillagon told Le Monde.

Cerutti went on to put his management skills to work in the art market, becoming head of Sotheby’s France in 2007. In 2015, he was poached by François Pinault, who appointed him president of Christie’s operations in Europe, the Middle East, Russia and India. Just months later, he was promoted to global chief executive of the auction house. At both Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Cerutti built a reputation as a formidable cost-cutter. He also proved adept at steering Christie’s through difficult market conditions.

His next move within the Pinault empire, however, was less successful. In January 2025, Cerutti was appointed president of the Pinault Collection, which oversees the Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice, as well as the Bourse de Commerce in Paris. Once again, he was following in the footsteps of Aillagon, who had held the same position in the 2010s. But, as Le Monde reports, Cerutti’s efforts to impose the kind of financial discipline he had introduced at Christie’s, coupled with his wish to slow the pace of acquisitions, brought him into conflict with Pinault, who was used to running his collection on his own terms. Barely a year later, Cerutti was forced to step down.

He now assumes one of the most coveted positions in French cultural life, taking charge of a historic palace, museum and gardens that welcomed 8.4 million visitors in 2025 and employ around 1,000 people. His extensive connections in the worlds of business, culture and politics could prove particularly valuable as Versailles faces mounting budgetary pressures and an ever-greater need to secure support from wealthy patrons.

“Man* is by Nature a migratory animal,” the elderly Frederick Douglass reflected in an 1887 speech about his global travels. “It does not appear that he was intended to dwell forever in any one locality. He is a born traveler.”

A generation after him, Maya Angelou observed that “you only are free when you realize you belong no place — you belong every place — no place at all.”

Partway in time between Douglass and Angelou, the painter, printmaker, and philosopher Rockwell Kent (June 21, 1882–March 13, 1971) captured this vital interplay between freedom and belonging, between nature and human nature, in the preface to Wilderness (public library) — the exquisite record of the seven months he spent on a remote Alaskan island with his young son in the gloaming hour of the Spanish flu pandemic and the First World War, at the dawn of his artistic life.

We each have a particular style of wanderlust, pulled by particular types of nature that best speak to our own — those places where we most freely lose ourselves and, in consequence, find ourselves. For some, they are the austere open space of blue skies and red canyons. For me, they are the mossy old-growth forests of New Zealand and the American Pacific Northwest. For Kent, it was the severe majesty of the Great North:

It has always been hard for me to understand myself, to know why I work and love and live. Yet it is fortunate that such matters find a way of caring for themselves. I came to Alaska because I love the North. I crave snow-topped mountains, dreary wastes, and the cruel Northern sea with its hard horizons at the edge of the world where infinite space begins. Here skies are clearer and deeper and, for the greater wonders they reveal, a thousand times more eloquent of the eternal mystery than those of softer lands.

In a new preface to his journals, penned in the final year of his life, Kent looks back on the wanderlust of his youth — the roaming restlessness that had shaped his spirit, the spirit from which his art sprang, the art that established him as one of the most celebrated creators of his time — and exhorts the generations of wanderers to come:

Wander where you will over all the world, from every valley seeing forever new hills calling you to climb them, from every mountain top farther peaks enticing you. Always the distant land looks fairest, till you are made at last a restless wanderer never reaching home — never — until you stand one day on the last peak on the border of the interminable sea, stopped by the finality of that.

Contemplating the existential pull beneath it all — the rippling, resonant why of our wanderlust — Kent adds:

We are part and parcel of the big plan of things. We are simply instruments recording in different measure our particular portion of the infinite. And what we absorb of it makes for character, and what we give forth, for [our art].

These are salutary words to read a century later, as our own world is only just shaking off its straitjacket of two-year terror and becoming wanderable again.

Complement with Rebecca Solnit’s wanderlusting history of walking, then revisit Kent’s breathtaking reflections on wilderness, solitude, and creativity.
